title: How To Build a Savings Plan If You Are a Full-Time U.S. Student
description: Leveraging low tax brackets and time to build wealth before graduation.
content:
Being a student usually means being broke. But if you have any earned income—from a summer internship, campus job, or side hustle—you have a golden opportunity. Because your income is low, your tax rate is effectively 0%. This allows you to contribute to a Roth IRA and pay zero taxes on the money ever again. Saving $100/month in college is more powerful than saving $500/month in your 30s. This guide explains how to start the wealth flywheel while still studying.

Key Takeaways

  • The 0% Tax Bracket: If you earn <$14,600 (Standard Deduction), you pay $0 federal income tax. This makes Roth IRA contributions mathematically perfect (Tax-free in, Tax-free growth, Tax-free out).
  • Earned Income Rule: You can only contribute to an IRA if you have 'Earned Income'. Allowance or gifts don't count. You need a W-2 or 1099 job.
  • Avoid Debt First: If you have unsubsidized student loans accruing interest at 7%, paying those down (or avoiding them) is usually better than investing.
  • The 'Buffer' Fund: Before investing, save $1,000 cash. You need liquidity for books, deposits, and car repairs so you don't use a credit card.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Kiddie Tax' applies to unearned income (dividends/interest) for dependents, but earned income is taxed at your own rate. Using a Roth IRA shelters your growth from future taxes when you are in a higher bracket.

The Student Wealth Stack

Prioritize your limited dollars.

1. The Liquidity Layer

Keep $1,000 - $2,000 in a High-Yield Savings Account.
Why? To avoid needing a parent bailout or credit card for emergencies.

2. The Debt Defense

If taking loans, calculate the interest.
Subsidized Loans: Interest is paid by Gov while in school. Strategy: Don't pay yet. Save cash.
Unsubsidized/Private: Interest accrues immediately. Strategy: Pay the interest monthly ($20-$50) so the balance doesn't grow.

3. The Roth IRA (The Magic Trick)

If you earn $3,000 in a summer job:
Put $3,000 into a Roth IRA.
Tax Paid: $0 (Standard Deduction).
Growth: Tax-Free.
Access: You can withdraw the $3,000 principal anytime if you need it for grad school or a house. It is flexible.

Hacks for Students

  1. The 'Parent Match': If you earn $3,000 but spend it on tuition, your parents can gift you $3,000 to put in your Roth IRA. As long as you earned the money, the IRA money can come from anywhere.
  2. Textbook Arbitrage: Never buy new at the bookstore. Buy used on Amazon/Chegg, then resell immediately after finals. Keep the difference.
  3. Student Discounts: Use your .edu email for Spotify, Amazon Prime, and software. Save the difference ($50/mo) into your investment account.
  4. Campus Jobs: Work-study jobs are often tax-exempt for FICA (Social Security) if you are a full-time student. This boosts your net pay.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I open an account under 18?

No. You need a 'Custodial IRA' opened by a parent. Once you turn 18/21, it converts to your name.

Does financial aid care about my savings?

Yes. Student assets are assessed at 20% for FAFSA. Retirement accounts (Roth IRA) are excluded from FAFSA. Saving in a Roth IRA hides the money from financial aid calculations. Saving in a bank account hurts aid.

What should I buy?

Total Stock Market Index (VTI). You have a 40+ year horizon. You can afford volatility. Don't buy bonds.
